## Overall project summary (end-of-course goal)

::: callout-note
This section describes where your project ends up **at the end of the course**.
It is not the to-do list for this milestone: see [Milestone 3 summary](#milestone-3-summary) for that.
:::

In this course you will work in assigned teams of three
or four (see group assignments on GitHub) to answer a predictive statistical/machine learning question
using a publicly available data set that will allow you to answer that question.
To answer this question, you will perform a complete data analysis in R and/or Python,
from data import to communication of results,
while placing significant emphasis on reproducible and trustworthy workflows.

By the end of the course, your project will have evolved from a single,
monolithic Quarto document into a fully reproducible and robust data analysis project, comprised of:

-   a well documented and modularized scripts written in R and/or Python,
-   a data analysis pipeline automated with GNU Make,
-   a reproducible report powered by Quarto,
-   a containerized computational environment created and made shareable by Docker
-   a remote version control repository on GitHub for project collaboration, sharing, and documentation.

## Milestone 3 summary

1.  Abstract code from your report literate code document (`*.ipynb`, `*.qmd` or `*.Rmd`) to scripts (e.g., `.R` or `.py`).
    This code need not be converted to a function,
    but can simply be files that call the functions needed to run your analysis.
    You should aim to split the analysis code into 4, or more, R or Python scripts.
    Where the code in each script is contributing to a related step in your analysis.
    Your scripts should take command line arguments.
    **You must document in your `README.md` how to call each script,
    including what arguments you pass each script.**

2.  Add data validation checks to your analysis scripts.

3.  If your report literate code document is not already a `*.qmd` file, convert it so that it is.

4.  Update your report so that it displays the figures and tables your scripts write,
    instead of computing them.
    You will polish the report's formatting in Milestone 4.

5.  Update your project's computational environment as you add dependencies to your project

An example Milestone 3 that corresponds to our expectations from this year is available here:
[Breast Cancer Predictor 2.0.0](https://github.com/ttimbers/breast-cancer-predictor/tree/2.0.0)

### 1. Abstract code from your literate code document (`*.ipynb`, `*.qmd` or `*.Rmd`) to scripts (e.g., `.R` or `.py`).

This code need not be converted to a function,
but can simply be files that call the functions needed to run your analysis.
You should aim to split the analysis code into 4, or more, R or Python scripts.
Where the code in each script is contributing to a related step in your analysis.

Below we list some examples of steps that your current report document can be broken up into.
It is not critical you split your code up exaclty as we list below,
but you must somehow split your analysis code up into 4, or more, R or Python scripts.

-   Download/extract data
-   Clean/transform data
-   Split and pre-process data
-   Exploratory data analysis
-   Model fitting
-   Model evaluation

The output of the first script must be the input of the second, and so on.
All scripts should have command line arguments
and we expect you to use the [`click`](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/8.0.x/)) Python package for parsing command line arguments for Python projects, and the `docopt` R package for parsing command line arguments for R projects.

They scripts could be organized something like this:

-   A first script that downloads the data from the internet and saves it locally.
    This should take at least two arguments:

    -   the path to the input file (a URL or a relative local path, such as data/file.csv), as well as
    -   a path/filename where to write the file to and what to call it (e.g., data/cleaned_data.csv).

    **Note: choose more descriptive filenames than the ones used above.
    These are general for illustrative purposes.**

-   A second script that reads the data from the first script
    and performs and data cleaning/pre-processing, transforming,
    and/or partitioning that needs to happen before exploratory data analysis or modeling takes place.
    This should take at least two arguments:

    -   a path/filename pointing to the data to be read in
    -   a path/filename pointing to where the cleaned/processed/transformed/partitioned data should live.

-   A third script which creates exploratory data visualization(s)
    and table(s) that are useful to help the reader/consumer understand that data set.
    These analysis artifacts should be written to files.
    This should take at least two arguments:

    -   a path/filename pointing to the data,
    -   a path/filename prefix where to write the figure to
        and what to call it (e.g., results/this_eda.png).

-   A fourth script that reads the data from the second script,
    performs the modeling and summarizes the results as a figure(s) and a table(s).
    These analysis artifacts should be written to files.
    This should take at least two arguments:

    -   a path/filename pointing to the data
    -   a path/filename prefix where to write the figure(s)/table(s) to
        and what to call it (e.g., results/this_analysis)

-   You are welcome to have any additional scripts as needed,
    or modify how you organize the splitting up of your code a little differently than suggested.
    What is important is that you have \~ 4 different scripts so you get practice setting them up in a data analysis pipeline (next milestone).

::: callout-important
**You must document in your `README.md` how to call each script,
including what arguments you pass each script.**
:::

### 2. Add data validation checks to your analysis scripts

To make sure that your data visualizations and modeling results are correct,
robust and of high quality, add data validation checks to your analysis.
Write them as code in your scripts,
for example as a step in the script that cleans or splits your data.
Ensure you cover the checks we recommend in our [Data validation checklist](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/data-validation.html#data-validation-checklist).
Write at least one check for each item in the data validation checklist.
Also be thoughtful about what you want to happen if/when your checks fail,
and be sure that your code reflects that.
Finally, when implementing your checks,
be sure they do not create data leakage between the training and test set.

### 3. If your report literate code document is not already a `*.qmd` file, convert it so that it is.

You can use `quarto convert notebook.ipynb` to convert Jupyter notebooks to `*.qmd` files.
If you were using an `.Rmd` file,
you can simply rename the file so that it has a `.qmd` file extension.
Much of the `.Rmd` syntax is backwards compatible, so this should mostly work.

### 4. Update your report to display your scripts' results

Your scripts now write your figures and tables to files.
Update your report so that it reads and displays those files,
instead of computing them itself.
You will polish the report's formatting
(table of contents, references, cross-references, inline values and hidden code)
in Milestone 4.

### 5. Update your project's computational environment as you add dependencies to your project

As you add packages to your project
(for example, `click` for your scripts, or a package for your data validation checks),
update your project's computational environment.
This means that your environment specification files will need to have these packages added, with the version pinned,
and the Docker container image will need to be rebuilt and published to DockerHub.

### 6. Update any instructions for running your analysis

Do not forget to update your project's documentation to reflect changes from this week.
Update instructions and/or commands in your `README.md`
and documention to run your analysis in your compute environment.
You may combine commands within `make`.
But instructions in the `README.md` file should include how to run the make target
and rule.

After you re-render your report,
copy it to `docs/index.html` again and push,
so the report on GitHub Pages stays current
(see [Milestone 2](milestone2.qmd#publish-your-report-on-github-pages)).

::: callout-important
## Your README instructions are worth 5 all-or-nothing points

5 points of this milestone are for the reproducibility of your README instructions:
whether someone can follow them to run your analysis, including each of your scripts, in your computational environment.
These points are all-or-nothing, and they cannot be recovered later.
If your instructions do not work exactly as you have written them,
you will lose all 5 points.

Make sure your instructions work on both Windows and Mac computers.
If your team does not have both,
work with another team to test them.
:::

## Submission Instructions

Just before you submit the milestone 3,
create a release on your project repository on GitHub
and name it something like `2.0.0` ([how to create a release](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository#creating-a-release)).
This release allows us and you to easily jump to the state of your repository at the time of submission for grading purposes,
while you continue to work on your project for the next milestone.

Follow the instructions for submission on Gradescope.
We only need URLs, entered into Gradescope directly: there is no PDF to make.
You will submit:

1.  the URL of your project's GitHub.com repository
2.  the URL of a GitHub release of your project's GitHub.com repository
3.  the URL of your report on GitHub Pages

## Expectations

-   **Everyone should contribute equally to all aspects of the project** **(e.g., code, writing, project management).**
    **This should be evidenced by a roughly equal number of commits,** **pull request reviews
    and participation in communication via GitHub issues.**
-   Each group member should work in a [GitHub flow workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/quickstart/github-flow);
    where they create branches for each feature or fix,
    which are reviewed and critiqued by at least one other teammate
    before the the pull request is accepted.
-   You should be committing to git and pushing to GitHub.com every time you work on this project.
-   Git commit messages should be meaningful.
    These will be marked.
    It's OK if one or two are less meaningful, but most should be.
-   Use GitHub issues to communicate to their team mate (as opposed to email or Slack).
-   Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense.
    It doesn't have to be complicated.
-   You should use proper grammar and full sentences in your README.
    Point form may occur, but should be less than 10% of your written documents.
-   **Your analysis should be correct,
    and run reproducibly given the instructions provided in the README.**
-   You should use proper grammar and full sentences in your README.
    Point form may occur, but should be less than 10% of your written documents.
-   R code should follow the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/),
    and Python code should follow the [black style guide](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/index.html) for Python)
-   You should not have extraneous files in your repository that should be ignored.
    The one exception is `docs/`: it is generated, but GitHub Pages needs it committed.
-   You will not be expected to incorporate Milestone 2 feedback in this submission (of course you can, but likely you will not receive it until the end of the week which might be too late to incorporate it).
